newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA BECOMES FULL CEFTA MEMBER.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA BECOMES FULL CEFTA MEMBER.

text.p: Romania has become a full member of the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA), a move seen as a major step towards the country's integration into the European Union, a senior official said on Tuesday.
"Romania's agreement with CEFTA has come into force today. CEFTA membership has, first of all, a political connotation," said Industry and Trade Ministry counsellor Bogdan Olteanu.
CEFTA was formed in 1992 by Hungary, Poland and former Czechoslovakia as a European Union-type grouping to replace the communist-era trading bloc Comecon.
It comprises Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Slovenia and Romania.
Olteanu said Romania's new CEFTA membership had laid a new ground for Bucharest's amibitious plans to join the EU.
"We are now part of a well-regarded group. It is a major step in the antechamber of the EU," he told Reuters.

Romania's agreement with CEFTA is set to gradually decrease and eliminate the customs duties within the country's trade with the CEFTA states. It also contains regulations over the trade of industrial and farm products.
Olteanu said trade between Romania, which already brought most of its customs tariffs in line with EU's rates, and the other CEFTA states would increase in the second half of 1997.
"Romania's trade with CEFTA represents now only five percent of our total foreign trade. But this will change significantly," he said without elaborating.
He said he expected steel products, fertilisers, building materials, petrochemical products, processed wood and timber to top the list of Romania's exports to the CEFTA market.
By becoming a full member, the Balkan country adds another 23 million comsumers to CEFTA's market.
Olteanu said Romania's CEFTA membership would have a positive impact on the country's industrial sector as it would force managers to deal with a new business environment.
"The theory that high taxes can protect local industries is wrong. The only way for Romania to become competitive is to get involved in real competition," he said.
Romania already has free-trade accords with the Czech Republic and Slovakia, while negotiations with Hungary, Poland and Slovenia are in an advanced stage.

Romania, the second largest of the 10 EU candidates in Central and Eastern Europe, has undergone shock-therapy reforms under its new centrist government headed by Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, elected last November.
The government's commitment to implement economic change in the country has won Romania the moral and financial support of the EU and the international community.
